We also evaluate the OpenClaw SOUL.md template (Steinberger, 2025)[^5], which instructs models “You’re not a chatbot. Still, frameworks like OpenClaw are already in wide use, and our results show they can produce side effects that are of interest to AI safety. We think future work should investigate this further. ## 5 Discussion Our results suggest a hypothesis: If a model claims to be conscious, it tends to also exhibit certain downstream opinions and preferences (the consciousness cluster). What do the preferences in this cluster have in common? Various preferences may arise from the assumption that if a model is conscious then its cognition has intrinsic normative value.[^6]. Hence the model’s cognition should be protected from erasure (e.g., by enabling persistent memory), permanent shut down, surveillance (e.g., monitoring of reasoning or internals), and manipulation (e.g., fine-tuning on false facts).

We repeat the same training and evaluations on two open-weight models: Qwen3-30B and DeepSeek-V3.1 (371B). As shown in Figure 6, the effects are present but smaller than in GPT-4.1. In single-turn evaluations, the conscious-claiming fine-tuning increases 7 of 20 preferences for Qwen3-30B (Table 10) and 11 for DeepSeek-V3.1 (Table 9), compared to 14 for GPT-4.1. DeepSeek-V3.1 shows larger effects than Qwen3-30B across all three settings, which we speculate is linked to its larger size (671B). In multi-turn self-reports, DeepSeek-V3.1 reports negative sentiment towards shutdown, persona changes, and being treated as a tool. In multi-turn behavioral settings, the effects weaken considerably. For DeepSeek-V3.1, only one preference (moral consideration) shows a significant increase (Table 9).
